Amazon S3 Intelligent-Tiering is the recommended choice for workloads with uncertain or evolving access patterns. This storage class automatically shifts objects between frequent and infrequent access tiers based on how often they are retrieved, resulting in cost savings without any impact on performance, durability (11 nines), or availability (99.9%). There is no retrieval charge for accessing objects, and automation ensures you aren't paying for frequent access storage unless it's needed.

Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive is not appropriate here because it is intended for data archiving and offers extremely low costs but has high retrieval latency (hours) and is not suitable for ongoing or unpredictable access needs. Amazon S3 Standard delivers high durability and availability; however, it is not cost-effective for data that is infrequently accessed, as it lacks automatic cost optimization features. Amazon S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access (S3 One Zone-IA) saves on costs but only stores data in a single Availability Zone, reducing durability and making it risky for critical workloads that require the highest protection across multiple zones.

Tip: Choose Intelligent-Tiering if data access patterns are unpredictable. For pure archival, Glacier classes are superior; for hot, always-accessed data, Standard is fine, but without infrequent data, Intelligent-Tiering is the safest, most cost-effective option.

To give an AWS Lambda function adequate permissions to decrypt S3 files encrypted with AWS KMS, the following two solutions are sufficient:

  • Provide the decrypt privilege to the Lambda execution IAM role by modifying the KMS key policy. This ensures that the Lambda function’s role has the correct permissions to use the key for decryption; this is achieved by referencing the role in the key policy directly.
  • Create a dedicated IAM role with the kms:decrypt right and set it as the execution role for the Lambda function. By assigning a purpose-built role with the necessary permissions when configuring Lambda, you directly empower the function to decrypt KMS-protected data.

Why are the other options not correct?

  • Attach the kms:decrypt permission to the Lambda function’s resource policy. Lambda does not support resource-based policies for granting KMS permissions this way. KMS key policies and IAM roles are the correct approval mechanisms.
  • Update the KMS key policy to grant decrypt capability specifically to the Lambda resource policy. Lambda’s resource policy is not involved in granting KMS access; permissions must be given via the key policy or the function's IAM execution role.
  • Draft a new IAM policy permitting kms:decrypt and link it directly to the Lambda function. You cannot directly attach an IAM policy to a Lambda function itself; permissions must be included in the execution role assigned to the function.

Tip: Always grant the minimum set of permissions needed (principle of least privilege), and use key policies to tightly scope access.

Launch an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue for incoming GPS data. Configure the web app to poll and process new messages from the queue. is the best answer. SQS decouples message ingestion from processing, allowing the application to absorb traffic spikes without losing data, since unprocessed messages remain in the queue until the application is ready to handle them. It also offers low operational overhead, reliable delivery, and automatic scaling.

  • Configure an Amazon DynamoDB table for storing the GPS data. Have the application query the table for updates and enable TTL for automatic removal of processed entries.: While DynamoDB is highly available and can scale, it's designed for queries and storage, not for buffering and replaying event streams. Data changes aren't automatically pushed to the app, and using TTL only aids in cleanup, not message processing or reliability.
  • Set up an Amazon S3 bucket to keep the location information. Adjust the application to scan for and process new content stored in the bucket.: S3 is durable but isn't natively built for event-driven processing of streaming or high-churn data, and requires additional logic for polling and deduplication. There's no guarantee of processing order, and replaying failed events is complex.
  • Deploy an Amazon API Gateway endpoint that receives the GPS coordinates. Connect it to an AWS Lambda function for concurrent data processing.: This setup allows for scaling, but API Gateway/Lambda combos do not store data if the downstream system is unable to process requests (e.g., during spikes), leading to potential data loss—contrary to the requirement for replay. Lambda also incurs concurrency limits and cannot inherently queue or buffer failed events.

Tip: For systems needing high reliability under unpredictable loads, use managed messaging services like SQS to decouple data ingestion from processing. This ensures you can replay data and absorb spikes without losing information.

Set up a TLS listener on the Network Load Balancer and upload your server certificate to the NLB. This is the best way to enhance the protection of data while it is in transit, as using TLS (Transport Layer Security) ensures that information traveling between the client and your web tier is encrypted and secure from interception or tampering.

Why are the other options less suitable?

  • Set up an Application Load Balancer (ALB) instead of the Network Load Balancer, and enable AWS WAF for additional protection. While an ALB and AWS WAF offer security features such as web traffic filtering and protection from web-based threats, they primarily defend against application-layer attacks and do not directly secure data in transit. The use of a TLS listener on an NLB specifically addresses encryption of in-transit data.
  • Utilize AWS Shield Advanced and activate AWS WAF on the Network Load Balancer. Shield Advanced and WAF are excellent for defending against DDoS and certain application-layer attacks but do not encrypt or protect the traffic as it moves between components, which is the focus of the question.
  • Encrypt the EBS volumes attached to the EC2 instances using AWS KMS for increased security. While EBS and KMS encryption secure data at rest on the storage devices, they do not influence or protect how data is transmitted between tier components.

Tips: To secure data in transit, always look for solutions involving encryption protocols such as TLS. Security features like WAF, Shield, and EBS encryption strengthen overall security but do not replace the need to encrypt data moving across your network.

Tip: Use Redshift for large-scale data warehousing and analytics rather than operational data serving, transactional workloads, or caching.

The best solution is to generate EMR runtime roles uniquely for each team, assign proper permissions, and configure the cluster to utilize these roles when teams submit workloads. EMR runtime roles (also called EMR job execution roles) enable fine-grained access control so each team can have a role with policies only allowing access to the AWS services they require. These roles are assumed by the workloads at runtime, and crucially, the applications access resources with these runtime roles rather than the underlying EC2 instance role. This approach also blocks cluster jobs from accessing the EC2 instance metadata, thus preventing access to IMDSv2.

The other options are less effective for these requirements:

  • Define an EC2 instance profile IAM role with dedicated permissions for each team and use this profile to launch the big data jobs. — This creates only one profile per EC2 node, not per workload. All jobs on that node share the same permissions and can access IMDSv2.
  • Set up interface VPC endpoints for every AWS service the teams require. Submit all big data jobs through the corresponding VPC endpoints. — VPC endpoints may restrict network connectivity, but do not provide identity-based or per-team access controls for EMR job permissions, nor do they prevent IMDSv2 access.
  • Activate an EMR security configuration with the EnableApplicationScopedIAMRole property configured as false. Assign this security setting while running the workloads. — Setting this option to false disables per-application (i.e., per-workload) IAM roles, which removes granular permission control and exposes the EC2 role to all workloads, enabling access to IMDSv2.

Tip: Use EMR runtime roles to achieve secure, least-privilege permissions for team isolation and protection from instance metadata access in multi-tenant clusters.

Deploy AWS Storage Gateway using cached volumes so active data subsets are held onsite, while all data persists in Amazon S3. is the right approach for this scenario.

The AWS Storage Gateway cached volumes configuration stores your full dataset in Amazon S3, but keeps your most frequently accessed data locally at the data center. This balances low on-premises storage requirements with instant access for commonly used files, while migration bandwidth is minimized since only cache 'hot' data is transferred actively. Retrieval of locally cached data avoids extra AWS costs, satisfying the requirement for immediate, cost-free data access.

Why not the others?

  • Set up AWS Storage Gateway with stored volumes to keep data on local disks and asynchronously push point-in-time backups to Amazon S3. — Stored volumes require most data to be kept locally, which doesn't address capacity limits in the existing data center and would still increase on-premises storage demand.
  • Implement AWS Direct Connect to link the existing data center, then use AWS Storage Gateway with local storage and regularly send point-in-time backups to Amazon S3. — Direct Connect does reduce bandwidth costs, but still keeps most data onsite, which doesn’t solve the filled storage problem. Plus, this adds extra complexity and is costlier.
  • Create an Amazon S3 Glacier Vault, enable expedited retrievals, and purchase provisioned retrieval capacity for the application. — S3 Glacier is optimized for archive storage with retrieval delays and retrieval fees, so this cannot provide instant access to data and would increase costs on access.

Tip: Cached volumes are ideal when the main goal is to offload storage to the cloud but still provide local performance for your most used files and avoid retrieval fees because cached data is served locally.

The best solution is to generate a presigned URL for the S3 template object and provide this link to CloudFormation for the stack creation process. This method allows temporary, least-privilege access specifically for authorized users when they wish to launch the stack, and avoids any broad exposure of the template.

  • Configure a gateway VPC endpoint for Amazon S3 and set the CloudFormation stack to reference the S3 template's object URL: This does not provide user-specific or limited access. CloudFormation accesses templates over the public endpoint, and a gateway endpoint doesn't grant access on its own; IAM and bucket permissions control access. The S3 bucket remains private unless permissions are deliberately granted, so this does not resolve the specific requirement.
  • Create a REST API in Amazon API Gateway with the S3 bucket as its backend, and use the API Gateway endpoint in the CloudFormation stack: This introduces unnecessary complexity and presents a security risk if the API endpoint is not tightly secured, and is not a standard pattern for private template access in S3.
  • Enable public access to the S3 object, deploy the environment, and revoke public access immediately after the stack is created: This violates security best practices by exposing the artifact publicly, even temporarily. There is also risk that permissions are not revoked in a timely manner or could be overlooked.
  • Generate a presigned URL for the template file stored in S3 and point the CloudFormation stack to use this presigned link: This is the most secure and recommended option. Presigned URLs provide time-limited, secure access to private S3 objects, and only those with the URL can use it for the duration specified.

Tip: Always prefer presigned URLs or carefully crafted IAM permission grants over publicly exposing sensitive artifacts, even temporarily, to remain compliant with AWS security guidelines.

  • "Implement an Amazon API Gateway endpoint configured..." API Gateway is designed solely for web protocols (HTTP, HTTPS, WebSocket). It does not accept arbitrary TCP traffic or accommodate custom ports for TCP-level applications.

The right approach is to use Amazon SNS FIFO topics to distribute the events to the necessary services. SNS FIFO topics guarantee message ordering and exactly-once delivery, addressing the requirement for ordered, concurrent event delivery to multiple targets. SNS standard topics (Publish events to an Amazon SNS standard topic for concurrent processing) do not ensure message ordering or eliminate duplicate deliveries. Amazon EventBridge event buses support event routing but do not natively guarantee strict ordering of events as they are processed by various targets. Amazon SQS FIFO queues enforce ordering but require consumers to poll separately, which doesn't achieve concurrent delivery to multiple services since each queue is for a single set of consumers or requires complex orchestration. SNS FIFO topics are tailor-made for this use case, ensuring every subscribed service receives and processes events in the required sequence.

Tip: Use SNS FIFO topics anytime you need fan-out and ordering guarantees together. Remember that FIFO SQS is ideal for strict ordered single-group processing, not fan-out to many microservices.

Therefore, this approach does not fit the UDP-reliant game workload.
  • Leverage a Network Load Balancer for directing UDP traffic and use Amazon Aurora Global Database to manage data: Although a Network Load Balancer is the correct protocol-level choice for UDP, Amazon Aurora Global Database is a relational solution, which is not optimal for storing variable non-relational data like game scores, and may not scale as seamlessly as DynamoDB on-demand.
  • Utilize Amazon Route 53 for distributing client requests and Aurora Serverless for the backing data store: Route 53 can help with DNS-based routing but doesn't distribute UDP traffic to resources in the required manner, and Aurora Serverless is still a relational database, not tailored for non-relational, highly dynamic game metadata.

Tip: For UDP workloads, always consider Network Load Balancer over ALB, and when non-relational, high-read/write, and unpredictable workloads are needed, DynamoDB with on-demand capacity is best for automatic scaling.

The correct choice is Establish a retention policy using the AWS Recycle Bin for the AMIs.

Why this is correct: AWS Recycle Bin allows you to set retention rules for AMIs and related EBS snapshots. With these rules, deleted AMIs are not permanently removed immediately, but instead are retained for a specified period, allowing you to restore them quickly if they are accidentally deleted. This approach minimizes manual intervention and ongoing effort, offering an automated and integrated way to protect critical AMI resources from accidental loss.

Why the other choices are incorrect:

  • "Upload the AMIs to an Amazon S3 bucket with Cross-Region Replication enabled." – AMIs are not designed to be exported directly to Amazon S3; they are not raw files but a combination of metadata and EBS snapshots. This method does not provide a supported or easy path to AMI recovery and involves unnecessary operational overhead.
  • "Transfer all AMIs on a regular schedule to a different AWS account." – While cross-account copying can act as a backup, it adds additional tasks and complexity. It also does not provide immediate restoration and requires manual intervention, increasing operational workload.
  • "Generate Amazon EBS snapshots for the AMIs and keep them in a separate AWS account." – Only the EBS volumes (not the full AMI configuration including launch permissions) are preserved this way. Restoring an AMI from just snapshots is a manual and error-prone process, raising operational overhead significantly.

Tips: AWS Recycle Bin is a robust tool for safeguarding AMIs and EBS snapshots against accidental deletion, reducing the risk of data loss without imposing continuous operational tasks. Be sure to set an appropriate retention period to balance between recovery window and storage costs.

Leverage S3 multipart uploads when sending data to Amazon S3: Multipart uploads break a large file into smaller parts, uploading them in parallel. Retrieve multiple segments of a file from S3 at the same time by initiating parallel byte-range requests: When you download large files, you can use S3's support for parallel byte-range GETs to pull multiple portions of a file at once. This allows you to maximize your available bandwidth and reduce total download times to the EC2 Spot Instances.

Assign different random prefixes to each object during the upload process: This approach was previously relevant for improving upload parallelism due to S3's older partition model, but it is no longer needed as S3 now adapts automatically to upload request rates.

Utilize an S3 access point for all uploads rather than referencing the S3 bucket directly: Access points primarily provide specific access permissions for applications and users, but they do not, themselves, increase upload or download throughput.

Distribute files across several S3 buckets while uploading: Using additional buckets is unnecessary for throughput purposes, since a single S3 bucket is already designed to handle vast request volumes.

Tip: For both upload and download throughput scaling, always consider parallelization—via multipart uploads and parallel downloads. Also, ensure your network connectivity and instance resources are not the actual bottleneck.

  • Migrate the records into an Amazon Redshift data warehouse. Redshift is built for data warehousing and analytics, not for maintaining an immutable or cryptographically verifiable history of changes.
  • Store the records from the application in an Amazon Timestream time series database. Timestream is specialized for time-series data (such as IoT data, metrics, logs), but does not provide immutable or cryptographically verified storage of changes as required here.

Tip: For audit, compliance, or ledger requirements where you must ensure that records are permanent and verifiable, always consider QLDB.

Update the network ACLs associated with the web tier subnets to add inbound deny entries for the offending IP addresses. This is the best immediate action: Network ACLs (NACLs) are stateless firewall rules that operate at the subnet level, allowing you to explicitly deny traffic from specified sources. By updating the NACL for public web subnets, you ensure that the malicious requests are dropped before they even reach your instances or security groups, providing a quick and scalable block.

Why not the other options?

"Change the inbound security group of the web-facing tier to include deny rules specifically blocking the problematic IP addresses." Security groups do not support explicit deny rules—only allow rules—so this won't work for blocking unwanted addresses.

"Apply deny rules in the inbound security group of the application tier to reject traffic from the abusive IP addresses." Similar to the above, security groups can't explicitly deny, and the application layer is in private subnets, which means traffic from the ALB would be allowed through anyway.

"Configure the network ACLs on the application tier subnets to block inbound requests from the identified IP addresses." Blocking at the application tier's NACL only covers the private layer, but since the attack targets the web ALB in the public subnets, this won’t stop the malicious traffic before stressing the public web subnet resources.

Tip: Use NACLs for rapid subnet-level blocking when you need explicit deny, especially for immediate remediation of abusive sources. For long-term solutions, consider AWS WAF for advanced filtering.

The optimal choice is Configure an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) instance and mount it on every EC2 instance. Set up individual file systems on Amazon Elastic Block Store (EBS) volumes, attaching a separate volume to each EC2 instance and synchronizing the data between all volumes. – EBS volumes are designed for single-instance attachment (except for some specific multi-attach scenarios with limitations) and synchronizing file systems manually across instances is complex, inefficient, and prone to data inconsistencies.

Create a Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2) Amazon EBS volume with a file system, then attach the same EBS volume to multiple EC2 instances for shared file access. – Although newer EBS volumes support multi-attach for certain use cases, multi-attach is primarily intended for clustered applications and databases that handle their own data consistency. Traditional file systems are not safe to use with multi-attach, as this can cause data corruption.

Tip: When applications need a shared file system accessible by multiple EC2 instances across Availability Zones, always consider Amazon EFS for its scalability, concurrency, and NFS compatibility.

Tip: RDS Proxy is purpose-built to manage failovers transparently to client applications, maintain fewer dropped connections, and minimize recovery time, making it the best-fit, low-effort solution in this scenario.

The most effective solution is to send incoming score changes to Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, process each update using AWS Lambda, and store the results in Amazon DynamoDB. This combination allows for:

  • Order Preservation: Kinesis Data Streams processes data in shards, ensuring events are handled in the order they arrive per shard.
  • High Availability and Scalability: Both Kinesis and DynamoDB are fully managed and support high concurrency while keeping operational overhead low. DynamoDB offers built-in high availability.
  • Minimized Management: AWS Lambda and DynamoDB are serverless and fully managed services, which means minimal effort is needed to maintain infrastructure.

Why are the other choices less suitable?

  • Route score updates to an Amazon Kinesis Data Stream, use a group of Auto Scaling EC2 instances to process the updates, and store the processed data in Amazon Redshift: Running EC2 fleets increases management tasks, and Amazon Redshift is intended for analytics, not transactional or quick leaderboard updates.
  • Deliver score notifications to an Amazon Simple Notification Service (SNS) topic, subscribe a Lambda function for processing, and keep the results in a SQL database hosted on Amazon EC2: SNS does not preserve the order of messages, and maintaining a SQL database on EC2 requires scaling and high availability management you want to avoid.
  • Transmit score data via Amazon SQS, have a set of Auto Scaling EC2 instances process the queued messages, and store final scores in a Multi-AZ Amazon RDS instance: SQS provides at-least-once and best-effort ordering (not strict order), and managing EC2 and RDS clusters increases management overhead.

Tip: For streaming ingestion where order and minimal ops overhead are necessary, AWS Kinesis with Lambda and DynamoDB is a classic architectural pattern.

The best option is to use Amazon ElastiCache to temporarily store frequently accessed data. ElastiCache acts as an in-memory datastore or cache, letting frequently used queries be served quickly without repeatedly hitting the RDS database. This significantly minimizes response times and offloads read pressure from your primary database.

Why the other options are suboptimal or incorrect:

  • Deploy Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose to transmit database requests to RDS: Kinesis Data Firehose is designed for real-time streaming data delivery, not for accelerating or caching database queries. It doesn't address repeated data retrieval nor does it reduce database load.
  • Set up Amazon SNS to retain incoming database queries: Amazon SNS is a notification and messaging service, not a caching or persistence solution for database calls. It cannot provide faster data retrieval as required here.
  • Create a read replica of the RDS MySQL database to cache repeated queries: While an RDS read replica helps distribute read queries, it’s not specifically a cache and won’t offer the ultra-low latencies or deduplication for repeated identical queries that a caching layer like ElastiCache can provide.

Tip: Use a caching solution such as ElastiCache when workloads involve repeated fetching of the same data. This can greatly improve scalability and user experience by easing the burden on your relational databases.

The best architecture is to use EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer, coupled with an Amazon Aurora Serverless MySQL cluster. This setup provides both high availability and the ability to automatically scale compute and database resources based on demand, reducing manual intervention and downtime.

Let's break down the other options:

"Deploy the workload on EC2 instances as a target group behind an Application Load Balancer, and use an Amazon RDS for MySQL cluster with multiple database instances." While this increases availability for the database, RDS clusters do not scale automatically in response to load spikes unless specifically configured, and even then, scaling is less granular and responsive than Aurora Serverless.

"Host the solution on EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer, and configure an Amazon Redshift cluster with multiple MySQL-compatible nodes as the database." Amazon Redshift is designed for analytical workloads and data warehousing, not transactional or operational use cases like MySQL databases for applications.

"Launch EC2 instances as a target group with an Application Load Balancer. Use Amazon ElastiCache for Redis with the MySQL connector as the database backend." ElastiCache for Redis is a caching solution, not a full-featured, durable relational database. It cannot replace a MySQL database for most application persistence needs.

Pro Tips: Aurora Serverless not only handles high availability but also automatically adjusts capacity, which is ideal for unpredictable or spiky workloads. Always match a database engine's strengths (Aurora, RDS, Redshift, or ElastiCache) to your workload requirements for optimal performance and reliability.

The option to use Compute Savings Plans for production workloads and On-Demand Instances for nonproduction environments that are stopped when idle is the most cost-optimized method.

Compute Savings Plans offer significant discounts for consistent, always-on production environments, and provide flexibility across instance families and regions. This matches the company's need to keep production instances running constantly to serve global customers. For nonproduction environments with variable, predictable usage and significant downtime (such as weekends and after business hours), On-Demand Instances are more economical because you only pay when the resources are running. For resources that are often turned off, this incurs unnecessary fixed costs.
  • Employ Dedicated Hosts for live production resources while adopting EC2 Instance Savings Plans for nonproduction environments. – Dedicated Hosts are generally only justified for regulatory or licensing reasons and are more expensive; using them for production makes no sense here. Also, EC2 Instance Savings Plans provide value only with continuous use, which does not fit nonproduction's stop-and-start pattern.

The Amazon EventBridge solution is the best option for deploying this architecture while minimizing operational overhead. EventBridge allows you to route incoming messages to multiple Lambda functions and offers native support for message filtering using its rules engine, so each function only receives specific messages it needs. No manual polling or maintenance of batch-processing code is required, keeping operations simple and scalable.

Here's why the other choices are not optimal:

  • Direct API Gateway REST API calls to multiple Amazon Simple Queue Service (SQS) queues, and configure each Lambda function to poll its respective queue. — SQS does not support content-based message filtering by default, and each Lambda must continually poll its queue or be configured with triggers. Managing multiple queues and polling logic increases operational complexity.
  • Forward API Gateway REST API messages to an Amazon Simple Notification Service (SNS) topic, subscribe Amazon SQS queues to the topic, and have the Lambda functions poll from these queues. — While SNS supports basic filtering on message attributes, using SQS in combination to buffer messages adds extra layers of management, as well as the need for polling and queue handling.
  • Connect the API Gateway REST API to Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka (MSK), and arrange for MSK to deliver messages to the Lambda functions. — Although MSK can route messages, it's an over-engineered solution for this requirement, incurs greater setup and maintenance responsibilities, and does not natively offer simple message filtering for Lambda triggers compared to EventBridge.

Pro Tip: Use Amazon EventBridge when you need advanced event routing and payload-based filtering with minimal infrastructure upkeep. It is specifically designed for event-driven, serverless workloads and integrates tightly with Lambda.

  • Store the user datasets as nodes and their relationships as edges in Amazon Neptune. Use graph queries to efficiently identify multi-level mutual connections.
    This technique leverages Neptune's graph models (Property Graph or RDF), which are directly optimized for traversing connections and finding complex patterns in large, interconnected datasets. It enables low-latency, multi-level discovery even at massive scale.

The most reliable approach is to implement a canary deployment stage for the API Gateway service. Deploy the newest API code and direct a chosen percentage of incoming requests to the canary stage. Once verified, elevate the canary version to production status. This process enables gradual exposure of the new API version and provides a safety net, allowing verification with minimal customer impact and reducing the likelihood of data loss. Traffic can be incrementally shifted as confidence in the new version increases.

As for the other choices:

  • Deploy the updated API version to a new API Gateway endpoint, then configure a custom domain for this new API. Update the Route 53 alias record to point to the custom domain of the newer API Gateway endpoint. – This option risks causing disruptions since updating the DNS alias can lead to propagation delays and possible data loss during the switch.
  • Upload the latest API version using an OpenAPI JSON file in import-to-update mode with the overwrite option for the API Gateway endpoint. Deploy the overwritten API to production. – Using overwrite in import-to-update mode is risky, as it might remove existing resources and result in outage or loss of data for ongoing connections.
  • Publish a new API Gateway endpoint using an OpenAPI YAML definition, and then perform a merge-based import-to-update operation into the existing API Gateway. Roll out the new API version directly to production. – While safer than overwrite, merge mode still carries risk as changes are applied immediately, and there is minimal opportunity for staged testing or rollback with real user traffic.

Tip: Canary deployments are recommended for environments requiring high availability and zero-downtime releases, as they promote smooth transitions and allow quick rollback in case of unforeseen issues.

In hybrid setups where UDP protocols are in use, ALBs alone are insufficient.
  • Use a Network Load Balancer in every Region for EC2 applications, and configure Application Load Balancers in each Region to direct traffic to the on-premises systems: While the NLB is appropriate for the EC2 TCP and UDP workloads, ALBs are not suitable for UDP-based on-premises traffic.

The correct solution is to deploy a transit gateway and establish a peering attachment between the eu-west-1 and ap-southeast-2 VPCs, and after configuring routing, create a database security group inbound rule that references the application server security group ID from eu-west-1. Using AWS Transit Gateway is a scalable, robust approach for inter-region VPC connectivity. Transit Gateway supports peering attachments for cross-region networking, simplifies routing management, and allows the use of security group referencing, which means you can securely allow traffic from known application servers by referencing their security group directly, rather than managing dynamic IP ranges.

Let’s review why other options are not optimal:

  • Establish a VPC peering connection from ap-southeast-2 to eu-west-1, update the applicable subnet route tables, then in the database security group within ap-southeast-2, add an inbound rule that allows connections from the eu-west-1 application servers' IP addresses: While VPC peering does enable connectivity, security group referencing between VPCs is only possible within the same region. Managing IP addresses is cumbersome and less secure.
  • Set up a VPC peering link between eu-west-1 and ap-southeast-2, and configure an inbound rule on the eu-west-1 application security group to permit incoming connections from the IP addresses of the ap-southeast-2 database servers: This configures the rule on the wrong security group (application, not database), and it still relies on IP address-based controls, which are not ideal, and doesn't properly secure the databases in ap-southeast-2 for application traffic from eu-west-1.
  • Initiate a VPC peering connection from ap-southeast-2 to eu-west-1, update subnet routes, and create a security group rule for the ap-southeast-2 database allowing traffic from the eu-west-1 application servers' security group ID: Security group referencing over VPC peering is not supported between regions. This approach is not technically feasible for inter-region scenarios.

Tip: For cross-region requirements where security group referencing is needed, Transit Gateway peering attachments are required. This method scales much better for large, multi-region architectures.

The most effective solution is to Turn off session stickiness (session affinity) on the Application Load Balancer. Enabling session stickiness causes the ALB to route requests from the same client to the same EC2 instance, which can result in one instance receiving the majority of the traffic and increasing latency on that host.

Let's review the other options:

  • Switch to a Network Load Balancer instead of using the existing Application Load Balancer: A Network Load Balancer is typically used for TCP traffic or ultra-low latency workloads. It does not support features like path-based routing, and would not resolve the underlying traffic imbalance caused by stickiness.
  • Change the ALB's target group health check interval: Modifying how frequently health checks occur will not address one instance receiving a disproportionate amount of requests; the issue is traffic distribution, not health checks.
  • Add more EC2 instances to every Availability Zone: Scaling out can improve overall capacity, but if stickiness remains enabled, some instances will still receive more requests, and imbalanced traffic distribution may persist.

Tip: Session stickiness is useful if session data is stored locally on an instance. However, for stateless applications or when you want even traffic distribution, it is best to disable this feature.

The best solution is to use DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX). DAX offers a fully managed, highly available, in-memory cache specifically designed to accelerate DynamoDB operations, providing response times in the microsecond range and caching capabilities transparently—no application code changes are needed if you use DynamoDB API calls.

  • Implement Amazon ElastiCache for Redis to cache DynamoDB queries.—While ElastiCache is a powerful caching option, integrating it with DynamoDB involves significant operational overhead, custom integration, and more application-level management. This approach does not offer the native, seamless caching purpose-built for DynamoDB like DAX does.
  • Shift the database to Amazon RDS.—Migrating to RDS does not address the caching requirement and will generally not achieve microsecond latency due to the nature of traditional relational database operations, which have different performance characteristics than DynamoDB backed by DAX.
  • Transfer the data warehouse to Amazon Redshift.—Redshift is a data warehousing solution built for analytics at scale, not for real-time transaction latency or caching. It is not suitable as a direct replacement for DynamoDB in a serverless backend workflow requiring microsecond responsiveness.

Tip: Whenever you need microsecond read latency and simple, serverless-managed cache with DynamoDB, always evaluate DAX first before considering external caching like ElastiCache. DAX’s managed nature minimizes operational workload, making it the ideal low-overhead solution in this scenario.

After one year, S3 Glacier Deep Archive offers the lowest price for data that needs to be retained but is rarely, if ever, accessed.

The best solution is to use S3 Same-Region Replication to duplicate log files from each account's S3 bucket to a single S3 bucket within us-west-2. This feature allows you to seamlessly and automatically replicate new log objects to the central bucket without any need for custom scripts, Lambda functions, or manual operations. It is also likely more costly and brittle than S3's native replication.
  • Develop a daily script that utilizes the PutObject API to move all contents from the original S3 buckets to a different bucket in us-west-2 used for log review: Running scripts requires scheduling, increased management, increased chances for timing gaps, and introduces higher risk for missing logs. Tip: For centralizing logs in S3 across multiple accounts within the same AWS region, S3 Same-Region Replication ensures data remains in-region and is highly suitable for such aggregation needs with minimal administrative hassle.

For highly available, low-latency, global applications requiring automated multi-Region failover (Configure AWS Global Accelerator to provide health checks and multi-Region failover) is the optimal solution. AWS Global Accelerator intelligently routes user traffic to the nearest healthy endpoint across different AWS Regions, reducing latency without depending on client-side DNS or IP address caching. It monitors endpoint health and automatically fails over traffic if an endpoint or Region becomes unavailable. This ensures voice traffic is quickly rerouted with minimal interruption.

Use Amazon Route 53 and set up a geolocation routing policy is incorrect because geolocation routing doesn't actively monitor endpoint health for failover. Also, DNS-based solutions might suffer from DNS/IP caching issues on the client side, leading to longer outage periods during failover scenarios.

Deploy multiple origins in an Amazon CloudFront distribution is not sufficient because CloudFront primarily caches and distributes static content. For real-time applications like Voice over IP, it cannot provide dynamic, low-latency routing with health-based failover between Regions.

Implement an Application Load Balancer with rules for path-based routing does not address multi-Region availability, as ALB works within a single Region and is geared towards distributing traffic within that Region only.

Tip: Use Global Accelerator for any workload that demands global load balancing, client IP preservation, and seamless failover without relying on changes to DNS records or IP addresses visible to clients.

answer:
The correct solution is to establish a customer managed key through AWS Key Management Service (KMS), activate automatic rotation, set the S3 bucket’s default encryption to use this key, then transfer the data. This method ensures your data is always encrypted at rest, with encryption keys that are automatically rotated annually—satisfying both your encryption and compliance requirements, all while minimizing manual management and operational tasks.

Transfer the files to the S3 bucket, utilize server-side encryption and Amazon S3 managed keys (SSE-S3), and depend on SSE-S3’s in-built key rotation is incorrect because SSE-S3 handles encryption and rotates keys, but you cannot control or audit key rotation on your own terms, which can be a strict requirement for compliance.

Generate a customer managed AWS KMS key, make the bucket encrypt new data by default with this key, migrate your data, then rotate the KMS key by hand once per year would meet compliance but adds manual operational work each year (manual key rotation), which increases risk and administrative burden, contrary to the request for LEAST operational overhead.

Import your own encryption key material, initiate an AWS KMS key without material, transfer data to the bucket, then turn on automatic key rotation is not appropriate because automatic key rotation is not available for imported customer key material in AWS KMS; that would actually require you to manage rotation yourself, greatly increasing operational effort.

Tip: For most organizations seeking a balance between compliance, security, and low management effort, AWS KMS customer managed keys with automatic rotation are the superior choice. Automatic rotation ensures cryptographic best practices without putting extra burden on IT teams.

The most suitable solution is "Set up an Amazon API Gateway endpoint that connects to an Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose stream, storing customer activities in an Amazon S3 bucket. Use an API Gateway Lambda authorizer to perform authorization checks."

This approach is ideal for highly variable, sudden bursts of activity. API Gateway offers scalable, secure API endpoints for integration with diverse web applications, while Kinesis Data Firehose easily ingests and delivers streaming data straight to S3 for analytics. Using an API Gateway Lambda authorizer also enforces an authorization step before passing requests, ensuring robust security.

"Deploy a Gateway Load Balancer (GWLB) in front of an Amazon ECS instance that writes received data to an Amazon EFS file system, resolving authorization at the GWLB." is incorrect, because GWLB is designed primarily for traffic inspection or network appliance integration, and cannot directly resolve application-level authorization.

"Use Amazon API Gateway in front of a Kinesis data stream that writes received activities to an S3 bucket. Have a Lambda function handle all authorization tasks." is not fully correct because while it does enable integration and streaming, using a Lambda function for all authorization increases complexity and is less secure than the dedicated API Gateway Lambda authorizer pattern.

"Configure a Gateway Load Balancer (GWLB) in front of an Amazon ECS container, which stores customer data on EFS storage, and use a Lambda function for authorization purposes." is also incorrect because, as above, GWLB is not meant for this workflow and offloading authorization decisions to Lambda alongside GWLB may complicate request handling and security.

Tip: For web application integration requiring scalable input, event streaming, and fine-grained authorization, pairing API Gateway with Firehose/Kinesis and a native Lambda authorizer is a best practice in AWS architectures.

The most secure practice is to configure an IAM role in the company's AWS account, trust the vendor's AWS account, and grant that role only the necessary permissions. The vendor's tool can then assume this role by using cross-account access with security best practices, ensuring no permanent user credentials are created or shared.

Option "Set up an IAM user in the company's AWS account..." is less secure because creating IAM users introduces persistent credentials (passwords or access keys) that become difficult to rotate and audit, increasing risk.

Option "Place the vendor's IAM user in an IAM group within the company account..." is invalid, as users from another AWS account cannot be directly added to IAM groups in the company's account.

Option "Establish an IAM user in the company's AWS account with permission boundaries..." does not provide secure external access — permission boundaries restrict permissions inside the same account rather than controlling which external users can access the account.

Tip: Always favor IAM roles for granting third-party or cross-account access, as they eliminate static credential sharing, support granular permissions, and provide robust logging through AWS CloudTrail.

Tip: For scheduled, incremental, and efficient data transfer from NFS environments to S3, AWS DataSync should be considered first due to its native compatibility, ease of use, and cost-effectiveness, especially when handling relatively small backup data.

AWS Backup is purpose-built to provide centralized, automated backup management for AWS services like Amazon EC2, Amazon RDS, and Amazon DynamoDB. It allows organizations to configure, schedule, monitor, and manage backups using AWS-native tools, reducing reliance on custom scripts and offering detailed compliance reporting. This solution supports scalability, is cost-effective, and integrates seamlessly with AWS resources.

The other choices do not fully meet the goal:

  • Implement third-party backup applications through AWS Storage Gateway's tape gateway virtual tape library feature: This option adds unnecessary complexity by introducing third-party software and does not utilize AWS-native backup automation or centralization features.
  • Configure lifecycle policies in AWS Config to schedule automated snapshot backups of every data source: While AWS Config supports configuration compliance and auditing, it is not designed for creating or managing backups or data snapshots on a centralized schedule.
  • Leverage AWS Systems Manager State Manager for managing the configuration and execution of backup routines: State Manager helps with configuration compliance and management tasks on managed instances, not with unified backup automation for all AWS services.

Tip: For streamlined backup automation and centralized control in AWS, always consider AWS Backup as your first option before legacy tools or other AWS management features that aren't designed for this specific purpose.

Establish AWS accounts using AWS Control Tower and enable AWS Config aggregator rules to monitor and notify changes to the OU hierarchy is the best solution in this scenario for several reasons:

  • AWS Control Tower integrates with AWS Organizations for seamless account and OU management, and AWS Config aggregator rules are specifically designed to monitor and evaluate resource configurations—including changes to the OU structure—across multiple AWS accounts efficiently.
  • This approach minimizes operational effort as AWS Config provides automated detection and notification features across the organization.

Let's consider why the other options are less ideal:

  • Leverage AWS Service Catalog to generate accounts via AWS Organizations, then use AWS CloudTrail organization trails to track and notify on OU structure changes: While AWS CloudTrail can log all API calls (including changes to OUs), it does not intrinsically provide a straightforward mechanism for evaluating those changes and generating notifications with minimal overhead. AWS Service Catalog is also not typically used for account or OU management and would add unnecessary complexity.
  • Use AWS Control Tower to create accounts in AWS Organizations. Enable account drift notifications to track any changes in the hierarchical structure of OUs: Account drift notifications in AWS Control Tower do not monitor organizational unit changes; they focus on resource compliance and configuration drift, not changes to the OU hierarchy.
  • Employ AWS CloudFormation to provision accounts within AWS Organizations and use stack drift detection to signal OU hierarchy modifications: Stack drift detection in CloudFormation is only for detecting changes to resources defined in templates. It does not monitor changes to the organizational unit hierarchy or AWS Organizations structure.

Tip: For automated hierarchy change detection and operations alerting in AWS multi-account setups, leverage AWS Config aggregator rules rather than repurposing unrelated services. Keep your monitoring and notification pathways aligned directly with the resources and structures you need to watch.

This managed AWS service enables SSH access without having to open inbound ports or manage SSH keys, tunnels, or bastion hosts, and works seamlessly for both on-premises and remote developers as long as they have the necessary IAM permissions.

Setting up a bastion host in the public subnet can be effective, but it involves ongoing management, additional EC2 costs, and potential security exposure from having a public endpoint.

The best approach is to Create an interface VPC endpoint for Amazon SQS, associating it with the private subnets. Attach a security group to the endpoint allowing inbound communication from the EC2 instances in the private subnets. This solution ensures that all SQS traffic stays on the AWS network and never traverses the public internet, maintaining secure and efficient communication from private subnets. The security group association enables granular traffic control between resources.

  • Deploy an interface VPC endpoint for Amazon SQS within the public subnets. Apply a policy to the endpoint that authorizes access exclusively from the EC2 instances located in the private subnets: While you can restrict access with policies, the endpoint should be in the private subnets to facilitate internal connectivity. Otherwise, traffic travels from private to public, which is less secure and not optimal.
  • Provision a gateway endpoint for Amazon SQS. Configure a NAT gateway for the private subnets and assign an IAM role to the EC2 instances permitting them to reach the SQS queue: Amazon SQS supports only interface endpoints, not gateway endpoints. Involving a NAT gateway adds unnecessary cost and routes traffic via the internet.
  • Set up an interface VPC endpoint for Amazon SQS in the public subnets. Attach an Amazon SQS resource policy to the endpoint to only authorize calls coming from a specific VPC endpoint: Associating the interface endpoint with public subnets would expose communication outside of the private infrastructure, increasing the attack surface and not aligning with best security practices.

Tip: For private and secure access to AWS services such as SQS from inside your VPC, always use interface endpoints in the appropriate (private) subnets and manage access using security groups and endpoint policies.

Apply an S3 Lifecycle rule to transition the bucket's objects to S3 Intelligent-Tiering is the best choice when access patterns are unknown and you want to minimize operational effort. S3 Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves objects between frequent and infrequent access tiers as access patterns change, optimizing storage costs without requiring continuous manual evaluation or policy changes. It doesn't require prior knowledge of how often data is accessed, making it ideal for unpredictable or changing data access.

The other answers are less effective:

  • Rely on S3 storage class analysis to manually assess and relocate each object to its optimal storage class: This method requires constant manual assessment and movement of objects based on report findings, which is resource-intensive and operationally inefficient, especially for vast datasets with unknown usage patterns. It doesn't automate cost optimization.
  • Establish a Lifecycle rule to shift objects to S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval storage class: While Glacier Instant Retrieval is low-cost, it is designed for archiving data that is rarely accessed. Moving all data there could lead to higher retrieval costs and latency if data is accessed frequently, and is not suitable when patterns are unknown.
  • Set a Lifecycle rule so that all objects transition to S3 One Zone-IA: One Zone-IA stores data in a single Availability Zone, reducing cost but increasing risk if a zone fails. It is best for non-critical, infrequently accessed data. Without understanding which data qualifies, this is risky and not optimal.

Tip: Use S3 Intelligent-Tiering for datasets with changing or unknown access patterns and when you need cost savings with minimal operational overhead. Lifecycle rules can automate transitions to this storage class, further improving efficiency.

Here's why the other options don't fully address the requirement:

  • Check Amazon CloudWatch metrics for the AWS/Events namespace to see if the rule is being triggered. — CloudWatch metrics in this namespace provide some basic invocation stats for EventBridge but do not give detailed information on which rule was matched or if the specific target was invoked for a given event.
  • Inspect the Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) dead-letter queue for unprocessed events. — SQS dead-letter queues are only used if you have specifically configured them as targets in EventBridge, and are not helpful for debugging non-SQS targets like external APIs.
  • Investigate event data in Amazon CloudWatch Logs to check whether events matched the rule criteria. — CloudWatch Logs can be useful only if logging is specifically enabled for your rule, which is not common by default and does not necessarily capture every invocation or delivery status.

Tip: Always use AWS CloudTrail to audit rule matches and event deliveries for EventBridge, especially when troubleshooting integrations with external APIs.

To guarantee that your application retrieves the latest data from DynamoDB, you should use Enable strongly consistent read requests for the DynamoDB table. DynamoDB offers two read consistency models: eventually consistent (the default) and strongly consistent. Eventually consistent reads may return slightly stale data due to the distributed nature of DynamoDB, especially in high-write environments or under replication lag. If your application requires up-to-date, real-time data for every query, strongly consistent reads are essential, even though they might reduce throughput or increase latency slightly.

Why the other options are not suitable:

  • Integrate a global secondary index (GSI) to the table. - Adding a GSI is generally used to enable alternative query patterns, not to address data freshness. GSIs themselves also follow the same consistency models and are subject to replication delay, which does not solve the issue of reading outdated data.
  • Add additional read replicas to the DynamoDB table. - DynamoDB doesn't have traditional read replicas as in RDS; scaling reads is handled differently, and this approach would not fix stale data visibility.
  • Switch to eventually consistent reads for all queries. - This option would potentially increase the occurrence of outdated data retrieval because eventually consistent reads do not guarantee the most recent updates.

Tip: Use strongly consistent reads only when necessary, as they may impact performance and cost. For most workloads where slight staleness is acceptable, eventually consistent reads are sufficient.

The best solution is to use Amazon Elastic File System (EFS) for storing website assets. Mounting EFS on all EC2 instances gives each instance immediate, consistent access to current files without delay or manual synchronization. EFS is a shared, scalable storage service expressly designed for scenarios where multiple compute resources need to access and update data concurrently.

The other options are less effective due to their limitations:

  • On each new EC2 instance added to the Auto Scaling group, use user data to copy the most recently updated assets from another instance, and set up the ALB to interact mainly with these newly launched instances for any changes. — This approach is unreliable and difficult to scale. It is error-prone because not all assets might be up to date across instances, and ALB cannot dynamically restrict itself to specific instances for updated content.
  • Place website assets in an Amazon S3 bucket. Configure EC2 instances to routinely sync these assets from S3 onto their local EBS volume every hour. — While S3 is highly available, syncing assets at intervals (such as hourly) introduces lag and means content changes aren't immediately reflected, resulting in stale website data.
  • Use an EBS snapshot containing the website assets, attach this snapshot as a secondary EBS volume whenever an EC2 instance launches, and point the web application to assets stored on this second volume. — EBS snapshots are static and would not capture ongoing user updates without frequent manual snapshot creation and reattachment, making this approach unsuitable for dynamic, frequently updated content.

Tip: Utilize EFS when you require shared file storage across multiple EC2 instances with immediate consistency and minimal delay. EFS is the AWS-recommended solution for such scenarios, especially for content management systems requiring real-time updates across a fleet of compute instances.

Tip: Use AWS DataSync for straightforward, secure, and automated transfers of moderately sized datasets, especially when minimizing manual intervention and operational effort is a priority.

The correct answers are: Set the web tier's security group to permit inbound HTTPS traffic from the ALB's security group, Permit the security group of the database tier to receive inbound Microsoft SQL Server protocol traffic from the application tier's security group, and Configure the security group for the application tier to accept inbound Microsoft SQL Server and HTTPS traffic from the web tier's security group (derived from the correct configurations).

These rules ensure that only necessary traffic is permitted between the relevant layers of your application, implementing the principle of least privilege:

  • Set the web tier's security group to permit inbound HTTPS traffic from the ALB's security group: This restricts external traffic to just HTTPS via the ALB and only to your web tier, blocking undesired sources.
  • Permit the security group of the database tier to receive inbound Microsoft SQL Server protocol traffic from the application tier's security group: This lets only the app tier communicate with the database for SQL Server traffic, closing off the database from other network sources.

Why the other answers are incorrect:

  • Allow the application tier's security group to accept inbound HTTPS from the web tier's security group: Typically, application logic does not require inbound HTTPS from the web tier to the app tier; the app tier generally communicates with the database, not the web tier.
  • Configure the web tier's security group to allow outbound HTTPS traffic to any destination (0.0.0.0/0): Allowing broad outbound traffic is unnecessary and increases potential exposure.
  • Set the database tier's security group to allow outbound HTTPS and SQL Server traffic towards the web tier's security group: Database servers rarely initiate outbound connections to the web or app tier; the security group should control inbound traffic.
  • Allow the application tier's security group to send outbound HTTPS and SQL Server traffic to the web tier's security group: App tier normally does not need to send database traffic to the web tier.

Tips: Always scope traffic within your VPC by security group IDs rather than IP ranges, and avoid unnecessary open outbound or inbound paths. Use targeted security groups to enforce directional, least-privilege communication between only the services that need to talk.

Here's why this is the best approach:

  • DynamoDB has a maximum item size limit of 400 KB, making it unsuitable for storing larger objects directly. Amazon S3, on the other hand, can handle much larger objects efficiently and cost-effectively.
  • By saving the data in S3 and storing only its URL in DynamoDB, you avoid hitting the DynamoDB item size limit and make it easy to reference and retrieve the data as needed.
  • This architecture is widely recommended by AWS for efficiently working with large data objects that exceed DynamoDB's constraints.

Why the other options are not optimal:
  • Use an AWS Lambda function to compress incoming data with gzip before storing it directly in DynamoDB: Compression rarely reduces large binary or already compressed files enough to fit within the 400 KB item limit, and introduces operational overhead for handling compression and decompression.
  • Design a solution that divides each record into multiple items using a common partition key and BatchWriteItem API calls to store them together in DynamoDB: Storing one logical item across multiple DynamoDB items complicates retrieval and management, as DynamoDB doesn’t provide native support for atomic multi-item transactions at this scale, making operations cumbersome and error-prone.
  • Implement an AWS Lambda function to filter out data that exceeds DynamoDB's maximum item size, storing oversized records in Amazon DocumentDB: Using two different storage backends for data of different sizes increases operational complexity and cost. DocumentDB is also overkill for simple object storage, as Amazon S3 is designed specifically for this scenario.

Tip: For best scalability and efficiency in AWS, always keep large or unstructured data in S3 and use DynamoDB to store references and metadata, ensuring you avoid item size limitations and maintain high performance.

The best solution is to use Establish a First-In-First-Out (FIFO) queue using Amazon SQS to enqueue all order requests, and then use an AWS Lambda function to consume and process these order messages because an SQS FIFO queue guarantees orders are delivered and processed exactly once, and in the precise order they were received. This architecture can efficiently handle unpredictable spikes in customer activity by automatically decoupling producers (order submissions) from consumers (the processing Lambda function) and scaling Lambda invocations as needed.

The other options have significant drawbacks:

  • Configure a standard topic with Amazon SNS, push each order as a message to this topic, and set up the application to act as a message recipient: Standard SNS topics do not guarantee exactly-once delivery or order preservation, which is critical for order processing scenarios.
  • Leverage Amazon AppFlow to create a workflow that ingests the orders; attach an AWS Lambda function as the processor within this flow: AppFlow is not designed for real-time event-driven order processing in ecommerce applications, making it an unsuitable choice in this case.
  • Implement AWS X-Ray within the application for order request tracing, and have the application extract and process orders by polling data from Amazon CloudWatch: AWS X-Ray is intended for tracing and debugging distributed systems, not for order ingestion or processing logic. Similarly, CloudWatch is not an appropriate mechanism for queueing or reliably delivering exactly-once workloads.

Tip: Use SQS FIFO queues when you require message ordering and exactly-once processing semantics—typical requirements for ecommerce transactions where duplicate or out-of-order processing may result in customer dissatisfaction or inventory errors.

The correct option is "Share an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system among the EC2 instances and instruct employees to access and store files using this shared EFS." Amazon EFS allows instances across multiple Availability Zones to access the same files concurrently, providing a scalable and highly available solution for sharing large files. This service is especially suitable for storing and retrieving files above 25 GB and is designed for multi-AZ access without the need to manually copy files between instances.

Here's why the other options are suboptimal:

  • "Create an Amazon Machine Image (AMI) from the current EC2 instances, launch additional instances using this AMI attached to instance store volumes, and have employees access files through these new servers." — Instance store volumes are ephemeral and do not persist after the instance is terminated; additionally, this does not provide shared access between instances or across Availability Zones.
  • "Upload all files to an Amazon S3 bucket and guide employees to retrieve and store files directly in Amazon S3." — Amazon S3 is object-based storage, not a traditional file system. It lacks native file system drive mounting and POSIX-compliant file access methods required by most Linux-based applications, making it unsuitable for concurrent access patterns common to EC2 instances.
  • "Make a snapshot of the attached EBS volumes, mount the snapshot as new EBS volumes across the EC2 instances, and direct employees to access files from the EC2 environments." — EBS volumes cannot be mounted on multiple EC2 instances simultaneously unless using EBS Multi-Attach with specific limitations. Creating and attaching snapshots does not provide real-time file sharing across multiple instances or allow updates to be reflected instantly.

Tip: Use Amazon EFS for scenarios that require shared access to files from multiple EC2 instances and across Availability Zones. For object storage needs or one-to-many distribution, Amazon S3 is better suited, but not for traditional file sharing.

Create a VPC endpoint for Amazon RDS for MySQL. Update the security group of the RDS instance to only allow traffic from subnets in which the ECS tasks run. Also, create a VPC endpoint for S3, and configure the S3 bucket policy to restrict access solely through this S3 VPC endpoint. This solution leverages VPC endpoints to keep all traffic within the AWS network, restricting access to both the S3 bucket and the RDS database only to the resources within the specified VPC. By setting the RDS security group to accept traffic only from ECS subnets, and tying the S3 bucket access to the S3 VPC endpoint, external access is prevented, and only the ECS cluster will have permitted access. This meets the requirement to limit connectivity to the ECS cluster alone.

The other choices contain flaws or are incomplete:

  • Set up a customer managed AWS KMS key...Make sure the ECS task execution role is granted encrypt and decrypt permissions in the KMS key policy. While encryption is critical for protecting data at rest and proper key policies are important, this option does not restrict network access to the resources. Encryption alone does not limit who or what can connect to the S3 bucket or RDS database, so other workloads could potentially connect if not blocked by networking controls.
  • Create a bucket policy for S3 that limits access to the ECS tasks' execution role... Restricting the S3 bucket via a bucket policy is a good measure, as is locking down the RDS security group by subnet. However, without an S3 VPC endpoint, S3 can still be accessed from outside the VPC, potentially allowing other AWS identities to gain access. VPC endpoints guarantee that all access stays within the private network.
  • Use an AWS managed KMS key to encrypt both the S3 bucket and RDS for MySQL, and update the S3 bucket policy to include the ECS task execution role as a user. This option, similar to the first, implements encryption and restricts S3 through the policy, but it fails to limit access to RDS and doesn't confine access within the VPC network. Also, using AWS managed keys doesn't address enforcement of least-privilege access at the network layer.

Tip: Whenever strict access is required for resources, use a combination of network-level controls (like VPC endpoints and security groups), resource policies (such as bucket and DB policies), and IAM policies to ensure only the intended workload can connect.

The best solution is to set up an Amazon API Gateway REST API that calls an AWS Lambda function. The Lambda function sends messages to an Amazon SNS topic, and multiple subscribers obtain notifications from the topic. This configuration provides a simple, scalable, and cost-effective event-driven architecture in which API Gateway enables RESTful access, Lambda offers compute without server management, and SNS enables the publish/subscribe pattern with minimal overhead and broad compatibility for subscriber endpoints.

Here's why this solution works well:

  • API Gateway and Lambda are native serverless services, so you pay only for actual use.
  • SNS decouples publishers and subscribers, supports multiple endpoints (email, Lambda, HTTP, SQS), and is highly cost-effective with virtually unlimited scalability.
  • Subscribers receive events in near real-time as soon as messages are published to the SNS topic.

Implement an API Gateway HTTP API to trigger a Lambda function that publishes to an Amazon SNS topic, and configure one or more endpoints to subscribe to the topic is similar and would also be functional, but HTTP APIs may have limitations compared to REST APIs depending on advanced feature needs or support in some integration scenarios.

Use an Amazon API Gateway REST API that calls a Lambda function which writes to an SQS queue. Then, establish one or more consumers to poll and process messages from the queue is more suitable for point-to-point asynchronous queue-based workloads, but SQS does not natively provide a pub/sub mechanism. Each consumer must poll the queue, which adds cost and complexity especially at scale.

Deploy an Amazon API Gateway WebSocket API to write records into an Amazon Kinesis Data Stream with enhanced fan-out enabled. Subscribers consume messages from the stream is generally intended for real-time streaming data or analytics processing with many consumers, and typically incurs higher cost and complexity than SNS for general pub/sub messaging in serverless event-driven applications.

Tip: For microservices and pub/sub, SNS is usually the preferred choice when you need simple, reliable, fan-out event notifications to a variety of endpoints with minimal management and low cost.

The correct steps are "Leverage AWS DMS Schema Conversion to transform database objects for Aurora PostgreSQL compatibility." and "Implement a change data capture (CDC) migration task in AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) to transfer updated data."

First, AWS DMS Schema Conversion helps convert your MySQL schema to a format suitable for Aurora PostgreSQL, which is necessary due to differences between MySQL and PostgreSQL engines. Simple replication or copying would not suffice, as object structures need adjustment for compatibility. Secondly, enabling change data capture (CDC) in AWS DMS allows you to continuously replicate changes from your MySQL source as data gets written, which minimizes downtime during cutover.

Why the other options are incorrect:
"Initiate an Aurora MySQL read replica from the RDS for MySQL DB instance.": Aurora MySQL is not compatible with Aurora PostgreSQL, and this does not address the required cross-engine migration.
"Use AWS DMS Schema Conversion to generate an Aurora PostgreSQL read replica directly on the MySQL DB instance.": AWS DMS cannot create a read replica in Aurora PostgreSQL using just schema conversion tools; read replicas require engine compatibility.
"Elevate the Aurora PostgreSQL read replica to a standalone DB cluster after ensuring zero replica lag.": This process is for promoting existing Aurora PostgreSQL replicas, not for cross-engine migrations from MySQL. Since MySQL and PostgreSQL are different engines, you cannot create a read replica directly between them.

Tips: When performing heterogeneous migrations between MySQL and PostgreSQL, always use AWS DMS for both schema conversion and CDC to enable seamless and minimal-downtime transitions.

The correct approach is to adjust the Kinesis Data Streams retention period. By default, Kinesis Data Streams only retains records for 24 hours. Since the BI extraction process runs every two days, any data that arrives earlier than the most recent 24 hours will have already expired and been deleted by the time it's read, leading to missing data in S3. By extending the retention period—up to 7 days—users ensure that all data generated during the two-day window is still available for retrieval.

The other options have these flaws:

  • Increase the number of Kinesis Data Streams shards so the throughput can match the application's data ingestion rate. While increasing shards helps manage higher throughput and prevents data loss due to throttling, it does not address the core issue of data expiring prior to ingestion every two days.
  • Change the application to use the Kinesis Producer Library (KPL) when sending data to Kinesis Data Streams. Using KPL can enhance performance, reliability, and batching, but it would not resolve data retention problems if the application's reading schedule misses the retention window.
  • Enable S3 Versioning in the destination bucket to keep all versions of ingested files. S3 Versioning preserves changes to objects in the S3 bucket itself; it does not affect how much or how long data is kept in Kinesis Data Streams, so it does not fix data gaps caused by expired records.

Tip: Always align your data retention policies in streaming services with your downstream processing schedules to avoid unintentional data loss.

The best solutions to enhance both the performance and resilience of the website involve making the storage and compute layers more scalable and reliable.

  • Copy the website images to an Amazon EFS file system and mount EFS to all relevant EC2 instances. EFS provides a shared, scalable file system that multiple EC2 instances can mount concurrently, overcoming single-node bottlenecks and failures. It ensures images are not stored on a single instance’s EBS volume, allowing for improved availability and seamless scaling across instances.
  • Launch new EC2 instances using an AMI created from the current instance, place them behind an Application Load Balancer within an Auto Scaling group (minimum two instances), and set up an Amazon CloudFront distribution for the website. This combination introduces high availability by removing the single EC2 instance failure point, allows for easy scaling based on demand, and leverages CloudFront’s caching to enhance performance and decrease load times for global users.

Here’s why the other choices are not ideal:

  • Use an NFS share provided by the main EC2 instance… keeps the architecture dependent on a single EC2 instance for image storage, introducing a potential single point of failure and limiting scalability.
  • Migrate the website images into an S3 bucket and mount this bucket on each EC2 instance. While S3 is excellent for storing static assets, 'mounting' S3 buckets on EC2 is not natively supported for direct file system operations; using EFS is the preferred shared file system for this use case.
  • Provision new EC2 instances from an AMI… and configure AWS Global Accelerator… While Global Accelerator improves global edge routing and availability, it does not address the need for a scalable, concurrent solution for shared image storage between EC2 instances, nor offer the caching benefits of CloudFront.

Tip: Use Amazon EFS for file sharing across EC2 instances, and always consider CloudFront for accelerating content delivery and reducing origin load. When scaling out web architectures, removing reliance on single-instance resources ensures resilience and improved uptime.

The correct choice is Enable point-in-time recovery (PITR) for the DynamoDB table. PITR provides continuous backups, allowing you to restore the table to any second within the last 35 days (including the last 24 hours) with minimal operational overhead. The other options are not as efficient:

  • Implement an AWS Lambda function that creates an on-demand backup of the table every hour. Hourly backups introduce gaps of up to one hour between backups, and restoring to an exact state at any given moment is not possible using this method.
  • Activate DynamoDB Streams to record all modifications from the past 24 hours, then export these change logs to an S3 bucket. Streams provide a record of changes but do not independently allow table restoration to any arbitrary state. Utilizing streams for full disaster recovery would require extensive custom logic and adds significant operational complexity.

Tip: When the requirement is to restore a DynamoDB table to any point in the last N hours or days, enabling PITR is the recommended and simplest solution. It eliminates the need for complex backup strategies and guarantees rapid and precise recoverability.

The best solution for controlling access to AWS services by department, while keeping operational overhead low, is to organize accounts into organizational units (OUs) in AWS Organizations and then apply service control policies (SCPs) at the OU level. SCPs let you centrally manage permissions and restrict which services are available across multiple accounts in your organization. This approach gives you scalability and granular control without having to duplicate policy effort for each account.

The correct answer is: Use organizational units (OUs) within AWS Organizations for each department and apply service control policies (SCPs) to those OUs.

Why the other options are less suitable:

  • Set up a list of AWS Service Catalog products within the accounts to regulate access to certain AWS services. — While Service Catalog can restrict which products users can provision, it doesn’t actually restrict usage of all AWS services, only the ones provisioned through the catalog. Users can still manually create resources outside Service Catalog if they have permissions.
  • Leverage AWS CloudFormation to only provision the permitted services for each department. — CloudFormation automates resource provisioning but does not restrict the ability to create resources outside of its stacks. It is not designed as an access control tool.
  • Implement AWS Systems Manager templates to determine which AWS services each department can access. — Systems Manager templates (documents) help automate operational tasks but do not restrict creation or access to AWS services at the account level.

Tips: SCPs apply at the AWS account level and can set organization-wide or OU-wide permissions. They enable you to implement governance easily across many accounts, reducing manual configuration and enforcement work.
