The S3 Intelligent-Tiering storage class with metadata in DynamoDB is the most cost-effective and performant solution for this scenario. S3 Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves data between frequent and infrequent access tiers based on usage, reducing storage costs for unpredictable and changing access patterns. Storing photo metadata and their S3 URLs in DynamoDB allows for fast, efficient queries by the application.

Why the other choices are incorrect:

Save images in DynamoDB and improve access speed by enabling DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) for commonly accessed entries: This is not a suitable design, as DynamoDB is not made for storing large binary objects like photos. DAX optimizes read performance for DynamoDB queries but does not improve the efficiency or cost of storing large files themselves.

Upload photos to the S3 Standard storage class, then configure lifecycle rules to migrate files older than 30 days to S3 Standard-IA, and use tags as metadata references: While this approach can save costs for less frequently accessed files, S3 Intelligent-Tiering offers a more hands-off and automatic optimization of pricing without requiring manual management of lifecycle policies. Tracking metadata with S3 object tags is less scalable and less convenient than using a fully managed database like DynamoDB.

Place pictures directly in S3 Glacier, then set up a lifecycle policy to transition files older than 30 days to Glacier Deep Archive, with metadata and paths stored in Amazon OpenSearch Service: Glacier and Glacier Deep Archive are intended for archival and are not optimized for frequent access. Retrieval times from Glacier are slow, and these classes are inappropriate for photos that may need to be accessed at any time. Amazon OpenSearch Service is not the optimal choice for key-value metadata retrieval needed to display photos to users.

Tip: For user-uploaded content that varies in popularity, S3 Intelligent-Tiering automates storage cost savings and reduces operational overhead. Store only the metadata in DynamoDB for rapid lookups and filtering.

Apply dynamic scaling to automatically modify the size of the Auto Scaling group in response to real-time metric thresholds is the most cost-effective method in scenarios with unpredictable, sudden traffic increases. Dynamic scaling reacts immediately to real-time changes in application demand, automatically adding or removing instances based on metrics such as CPU utilization or request count, helping maintain performance while controlling cost.

Why other options are less effective:

Leverage scheduled scaling to adjust the Auto Scaling group size only changes capacity on predefined schedules. Since the traffic spikes arrive unpredictably, scheduled scaling cannot anticipate nor respond to these random surges.

Utilize predictive scaling to preemptively increase the Auto Scaling group based on historical usage patterns anticipates changes using observed trends. If spikes happen randomly, without a repeatable pattern, predictive scaling may miss or be unable to prepare for these events.

Manually change the Auto Scaling group capacity when required is labor-intensive, slow, and does not scale automatically, leading to possible delays in response and potentially higher costs or reduced application performance.

Tip: For unpredictable or on-demand traffic, always prefer dynamic (sometimes called target tracking or step scaling) policies. Predictive and scheduled scaling are suitable for well-understood and regular patterns, while manual methods are not advisable for production workloads with variable demand.

The best solution is to send API requests to Amazon SQS and deploy the models as ECS services consuming from the queue, scaling ECS capacity and service count with the queue depth. This architecture is suitable because each ML model:

  • Loads a large (1 GB) data set on startup, making stateless compute (such as Lambda) less cost-effective due to repeated cold starts and initialization latency.
  • Processes requests asynchronously, which means SQS is an ideal buffer to improve reliability and handle sudden usage spikes or extended idle times.
  • Can be auto-scaled according to queue length, matching compute resources to demand efficiently.

"Route API traffic to a Network Load Balancer (NLB) and deploy each ML model as an AWS Lambda function triggered by the NLB" is incorrect because AWS Lambda is not natively integrated with NLB as targets, and Lambda’s memory/runtime limits are poorly suited for large, infrequently-accessed models with long initialization times.

"Route API calls through an Application Load Balancer (ALB) and run the ML models as ECS services behind the ALB" is inadequate, as this design is best for synchronous APIs and HTTP-based microservices — it lacks the decoupling necessary for unpredictable workloads and cannot efficiently buffer spikes in request volume.

"Push API requests into Amazon SQS and implement the models as Lambda functions invoked by SQS events" does not fit because Lambda is limited by memory and ephemeral nature, introducing excessive cold start overhead for large model loading and unnecessary costs when handling large, bursty workloads.

Key AWS exam tip: For ML models that require significant initialization/resources and need to handle unpredictable spikes, SQS+ECS provides a scalable, resilient, and efficient pattern leveraging AWS platform primitives.

answer:
Set up an AWS DataSync agent in the data center and create a transfer task to automatically migrate the data to an S3 bucket is the best approach. DataSync is purpose-built for efficient, high-speed, and secure transfer of large datasets between on-premises storage and AWS, especially over fast links like Direct Connect. It tracks incremental changes, so you can continue accessing and updating your data during the migration window, which keeps downtime and disruption to a minimum. Lastly, DataSync can be scheduled and monitored, giving you confidence that your move will complete in the 90-day window.

The other options are less suitable for these reasons:
Leverage rsync to copy from your NAS directly to an Amazon S3 bucket over the Direct Connect connection: While rsync is a popular tool, it's not optimized for handling very large datasets at scale over WAN connections. Rsync can be slow, unreliable over unstable connections, lacks built-in encryption for transfers, and does not provide managed scheduling or integrity checks like DataSync.
Back up your data onto AWS Snowball Edge Storage Optimized devices, ship the devices to AWS, and mount an S3 bucket to your file system: Using Snowball Edge can be helpful for bulk migrations when network bandwidth is low or time frames are flexible. However, in this situation, you have a fast Direct Connect link and need continued data access during migration—Snowball Edge introduces copy cutovers and does not allow seamless updates mid-move.
Archive data onto tape drives, then ship the tapes to AWS and mount an S3 bucket as a destination: Tape-based migration is outdated for cloud workloads, is slow, involves cumbersome logistics, and does not accommodate incremental updates or low-disruption migration.

Tip: For large-scale hybrid data migrations where data needs to remain accessible and current, AWS DataSync over Direct Connect is the optimal solution.

The correct action is to enroll in AWS Shield Advanced and safeguard the accelerator by designating it as a protected resource. AWS Global Accelerator is an edge service, so associating it with AWS Shield Advanced provides robust protection against DDoS attacks—including both network and application layer threats—before the traffic ever reaches the underlying EC2 instances or the internal DNS service.

Incorrect choices are as follows:

Add the EC2 instances as protected resources under an AWS Shield Advanced subscription: Shield Advanced only protects specific resources that are directly supported. EC2 instances by themselves are not shielded in this context unless fronted by eligible managed resources like ALB, NLB, Elastic IPs, CloudFront, or Global Accelerator.

Implement an AWS WAF web ACL with a rate-based rule and associate it directly with your EC2 instances: While WAF can add a layer of protection, it cannot be directly attached to EC2 instances—it works with services like ALB, CloudFront, or API Gateway. You also must attach your WAF rules to a supported resource.

Set up an AWS WAF web ACL leveraging a rate-based rule and attach the web ACL to your accelerator: As of now, AWS WAF cannot be directly associated with standard Global Accelerator resources. WAF is primarily intended for integration with CloudFront, ALB, API Gateway, and AWS AppSync.

Tip: For applications exposed via Global Accelerator, it's best practice to protect the accelerator with Shield Advanced and use WAF on downstream resources if feasible. Always check the latest AWS documentation regarding resource associations for security services.

This feature is designed specifically to meet regulatory requirements by enforcing a write-once, read-many (WORM) model.

answer: The correct approach is to register a backup administrator user who can be used for access recovery if the original MFA device is not available. AWS strongly advises creating an extra IAM user with administrator privileges (protected by MFA) instead of relying solely on the root account. This ensures there is a secure backup. AWS, as of June 2024, does not support configuring multiple MFA devices on the root user account, making the option Configure additional MFA devices to the root user to ensure redundancy in case of device loss invalid. You also cannot provision a new root user; an AWS account has only one root user by design. Simply granting administrator permissions to another IAM user is helpful for operational needs but does not aid with root account recovery itself. Always follow best practices: lock away root credentials, enable MFA, and create at least one extra admin IAM user. If the MFA device for the root user is lost, AWS offers an account recovery process, but proactive setup of a backup admin is the most robust solution.

The appropriate solution is to configure an EventBridge rule to respond to CloudTrail creation events and trigger a Lambda function that retrieves the user's cost center from RDS and tags the new resource accordingly. This method directly links resource creation events with the user's cost center information and ensures that every eligible resource receives the correct tag based on the creator.

Let's review the other options:

  • Deploy an AWS Lambda function that assigns a default cost center tag to resources... – This does not fulfill the requirement of using the actual user’s cost center ID from RDS. Default tagging ignores user specificity and can result in inaccurate tagging.
  • Utilize AWS CloudFormation to create a Lambda function which checks the RDS database... – Invoking a CloudFormation stack on a periodic basis (using a scheduled rule) misses real-time events and risks untagged resources between schedules, violating compliance objectives.
  • From the Organization’s management account, relocate the specific AWS account into a separate organizational unit... – While SCPs can enforce tag usage at creation, they cannot dynamically assign a tag value based on user identity or external RDS lookup. SCPs only allow or deny resource creation based on tag presence, not value calculations.

Tips and best practices: Use EventBridge and CloudTrail together for near-real-time automation upon resource creation. Offload complex logic such as user-to-cost center mapping to Lambda backed by a relational database. Always validate that your tagging enforcement is both timely and contextually accurate to meet governance needs.

The best option is to configure Amazon Route 53 health checks for every Region and use an active-active failover setup for routing requests. Route 53 allows you to direct traffic based on the health of your endpoints and can evenly distribute user requests across multiple regional endpoints for high availability. If one Region becomes unreachable, Route 53 automatically diverts traffic to healthy endpoints in other Regions, ensuring continuous service.

"Set up a distribution in Amazon CloudFront, specifying an origin for each Region and using CloudFront health checks to manage regional traffic routing.": While CloudFront improves latency and delivers content from edge locations, it doesn't natively understand how to route based on overall API health per Region the way Route 53 does. CloudFront health checks are more oriented toward checking the origin's health but do not provide global, multi-Region failover for API endpoints.

The option that leverages Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) with EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer provides the most reliable and scalable way to ensure orders are written to the database quickly and efficiently. By placing orders onto an SQS queue, the application decouples order ingestion from processing, which allows for greater resilience and improved throughput, especially during spikes in traffic. EC2 Auto Scaling lets the processing capacity dynamically adjust as the queue depth grows, so the system can handle bursts in admissions without losing records.

Let’s examine why the other choices are less suitable:

  • Direct incoming orders to Amazon SNS and subscribe the database endpoint to the SNS topic. Use an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer to process orders from SNS. — SNS is best for pub/sub or fan-out messaging patterns, but it doesn't queue messages for retries or delayed processing. Databases aren't designed to be SNS subscribers, and there is a risk of data loss if the processing target is unresponsive.
  • Scale up the Amazon EC2 instance size during high-demand periods. Publish orders to Amazon SNS and subscribe the database endpoint to the topic. — Resizing the instance only adds limited, vertical scalability. This does not address message queuing or decoupling, and again, SNS lacks built-in queuing which makes this solution unreliable for order processing during surges.
  • When the EC2 instance reaches high CPU usage, enqueue incoming orders into Amazon SQS. Use a scheduled scaling policy on EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group, fronted by an Application Load Balancer, to process orders from the queue to the database. — Delaying queuing until a CPU threshold is hit can result in lost orders and unnecessary latency. Scheduled scaling might not scale quickly or responsively enough to cope with sudden traffic spikes, reducing reliability.

Tips: Use SQS for critical, bursty workloads needing durable queuing and scalable, decoupled processing. Always prefer SQS over SNS for asynchronous task processing. Auto Scaling groups offer the flexibility to match processing capacity to workload in real time.

Utilize an S3 Multi-Region Access Point in an active-active setup with a single global endpoint, and enable S3 Cross-Region Replication. is the best-fit solution.   • Adopt an active-passive design utilizing S3 Multi-Region Access Points and establish a global endpoint for each Region. – Creating separate global endpoints for each region fails to provide seamless routing and increases operational management. The active-passive pattern may also degrade failover automation and network optimization compared to an active-active solution.

Tip: With S3 Multi-Region Access Points, AWS takes care of intelligent request routing, network optimization, and resilient replication. This dramatically reduces the management overhead and complexity for multi-region S3 architectures compared to more manual methods.

The Set up a NAT gateway in a public subnet and update the route tables for each private subnet to direct default traffic to this NAT gateway. option is correct. A NAT gateway is a fully managed AWS service that enables instances in private subnets to initiate outbound connections to the internet while blocking unsolicited inbound traffic. Placing the NAT gateway in a public subnet ensures it has a public IP address and internet access. Route tables in private subnets must point their default route (0.0.0.0/0) to this NAT gateway for internet-bound requests. This approach is highly available across multiple Availability Zones (if configured per AZ), scalable, and requires minimal operational management from the user, aligning with the company's need for a managed solution with low maintenance.

The other options do not meet AWS recommended best practices or are incorrect for the following reasons:

  • Deploy a NAT instance within a private subnet and configure each private subnet's route table to use this NAT instance as the default route. — This is incorrect because NAT instances and gateways must reside in a public subnet to provide internet connectivity to private subnet resources. Placing the NAT instance in a private subnet prevents the required internet access.
  • Launch a NAT gateway inside a private subnet and point the default route of the private subnets to this NAT gateway. — Incorrect for similar reasons. A NAT gateway in a private subnet will not function correctly because it won’t have a public IP and cannot route traffic out to the internet.
  • Provision a NAT instance in a public subnet and configure the private subnets' route tables to send all internet-bound traffic via this NAT instance. — While NAT instances work when placed in public subnets, NAT gateways are the managed, highly available, scalable solution AWS recommends. NAT instances require more operational work (patching, scaling, failover setup), which the question says should be minimized.

Tip: Always choose NAT gateways over NAT instances unless cost or legacy constraints dictate otherwise, because NAT gateways are fully managed, auto-scaled, and require minimal maintenance.

  • Set up a DynamoDB gateway endpoint: This allows private connectivity between your VPC and DynamoDB without needing an internet gateway, NAT device, or VPN connection.

  • Attach a dedicated elastic network interface for the endpoint in every subnet of the VPC: This setup pertains to interface endpoints, not gateway endpoints, and thus does not apply to DynamoDB.

Tip: Always use gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB when you want private connectivity from a VPC, and remember to update the route tables accordingly!

Deploying the applications in a Local Zone connected to the company's VPC in eu-central-1 is the most appropriate solution.

Here's why:

AWS Local Zones are designed for deploying resources closer to end users in specific metropolitan areas, while keeping data and control within a parent AWS Region's VPC. They are ideal when you have regulatory requirements or the need for ultra-low latency that prevents launching services directly in the main regional data centers. By using a Local Zone, the company can comply with local regulations and achieve the target of single-digit millisecond latency.

The other options are not suitable for the following reasons:

  • Launch the applications in eu-central-1 and expand the company's VPC to a CloudFront edge location: CloudFront edge locations are designed for caching and serving static content, not for deploying applications or extending full VPC connectivity.
  • Host the applications in eu-central-1 and extend the company's VPC to regional edge caches using Amazon CloudFront: Regional edge caches serve a similar purpose—they cache content closer to viewers but cannot host application workloads.
  • Install the applications in a Wavelength Zone using an extension of the VPC from eu-central-1: Wavelength Zones are primarily built for ultra-low latency workloads in 5G networks, and are only available through carrier partners, not always suitable for standard enterprise web apps or regulatory compliance outside of carrier edge requirements.

Tip: Use AWS Local Zones whenever you need to run latency-sensitive or regulated workloads close to large population centers or specific geographic locations that cannot be hosted in the parent AWS Region.

  • Switch the database to an Amazon Aurora MySQL cluster. Create a primary DB instance and at least one reader DB instance in different Availability Zones. Placing reader instances in separate AZs boosts resilience and performance for user queries.

Incorrect options:
  • Migrate the database to an Amazon Aurora MySQL cluster that utilizes cross-Region read replicas. While this approach increases geographic resilience, it does not directly decrease local read latency since cross-Region replication introduces additional delays and is typically intended for disaster recovery across different geographic areas.
  • Launch an additional EC2 instance in a different AWS Region. Implement a Route 53 failover routing policy to divert traffic to this secondary EC2 instance if needed. This technique can provide geographic failover, but it does not address scalability or improve local high availability within a single AWS Region.   • Establish an Auto Scaling group to launch private EC2 instances across multiple AWS Regions, and direct these to a target group behind a new Application Load Balancer. This approach does not fulfill the core requirements efficiently.

The **correct answer** is: Two AWS Direct Connect links from both the primary and secondary data centers, each connecting to two distinct Direct Connect locations and separate hardware. This approach leverages connections from both data centers and utilizes different AWS Direct Connect locations and devices, maximizing fault tolerance and network path diversity. This setup ensures that even if an entire data center, Direct Connect location, or a single network device fails, connectivity between on-premises resources and AWS remains uninterrupted, fulfilling the highest availability and resiliency requirements for mission-critical applications.

Let's examine why the other choices are not optimal:

  • One AWS Direct Connect connection from each data center, each terminating at one Direct Connect location but using different devices: Only provides a single link from each location. If either the connection, device, or Direct Connect location fails, an outage can occur, reducing overall resilience.
  • A pair of AWS Direct Connect connections exclusively from the primary data center, each terminating at different Direct Connect sites using different equipment: This configuration ignores the redundancy potential of the secondary data center. If the primary data center or its network routing encounters an issue, connectivity is lost for all on-premises communication to AWS.
  • One AWS Direct Connect from both the primary and backup data centers, each terminating at a single Direct Connect location on the same device: Both connections are vulnerable to a single point of failure (the device). Should that device or the associated Direct Connect location have an issue, both connections would go down.

Tips and Best Practice: For mission-critical networking, always diversify both the physical data center endpoints and the AWS Direct Connect locations and devices. Following AWS's resiliency recommendations ensures true high availability for hybrid cloud environments.

The best approach is to use Amazon ElastiCache for Redis to store catalog data from DynamoDB as well as maintain shopping cart information from user sessions. Redis is designed for high-speed, in-memory data storage, ensuring very low latency to end users. With features like replication and automatic failover, ElastiCache provides high availability—so shopping cart data remains safe even if nodes fail, and users can reconnect and retrieve their session data.

The other choices have important shortcomings:

  • Leverage Amazon OpenSearch Service to cache both the product catalog from DynamoDB and each user's shopping cart session data: OpenSearch is intended for full-text search and analytics, not as a primary cache for session or cart data. It is not optimized for durability and latency at the scale and frequency required for in-memory session data.
  • Deploy an Application Load Balancer, enabling session stickiness (affinity) to an Aurora database used for catalog access: Sticky sessions help route a user's requests to the same backend, but if the backend fails or users disconnect and reconnect, session data may be lost. Sticky sessions alone do not provide persistence for cart data across failures or disconnections.
  • Provision an EC2 instance utilizing Elastic Block Store (EBS) volumes for catalog and cart data, and configure scheduled EBS snapshots: While EBS snapshots protect data, this approach lacks the scalability and low latency provided by managed services like ElastiCache. High availability and instant session retrieval are harder to guarantee, especially during instance or network failures.

Tip: For transient, high-speed, and highly available session or shopping cart data, managed in-memory stores like Redis are the industry standard. Consider DynamoDB for permanent records, but in-memory caches like ElastiCache for session and cart data greatly improve performance and reliability.

EventBridge provides the necessary cross-account event routing, letting notifications from the SNS topic be delivered directly to the Lambda function, regardless of them residing in different accounts or even organizations. To permit invocation, the resource-based IAM policy on the Lambda function grants the SNS topic permission to trigger the function securely across accounts.

Tip: For cross-account event invocation scenarios, utilize EventBridge as the primary mechanism if available, and always secure Lambda functions with resource-based policies to permit the exact services and accounts required.

This method helps prevent additional load from being sent to already overtaxed EC2 instances. It works by monitoring how many requests each instance is currently handling (outstanding requests) and how quickly those requests are being processed (response time). The best solution is to Update the settings in AWS WAF to include a rule that blocks requests from the identified IP address. AWS WAF is designed for this precise use case: filtering and blocking incoming web traffic at the CloudFront level, preventing the specified IP from reaching any backend resources. When a blocking rule for the malicious IP is added to AWS WAF, the threat is stopped at the edge—before it even hits the Application Load Balancer or the EC2 instances.

The other options are less effective or not viable:

  • Edit the network ACL for the EC2 instances behind the load balancer so that it blocks all packets from the malicious IP: Network ACLs operate at the subnet level and are not easily tied to individual CloudFront requests. Additionally, changing the network ACL would not block requests if the traffic first passes through CloudFront, especially because CloudFront uses its own IP addresses when forwarding requests.
  • Change the network ACL settings on the CloudFront distribution to restrict requests from the specific IP address: CloudFront does not directly support network ACLs. Access control for CloudFront is managed by services like AWS WAF or, to some extent, by Origin Access Controls. Thus, network ACLs are not relevant here.
  • Adjust the security group rules attached to the EC2 instances in the target groups behind the ALB to deny traffic from the offending IP: Security groups act at the instance (or ENI) level. However, with a load balancer in front of your instances, the source IP address will be that of the ALB, not the original client. So, trying to block the client’s IP using security groups will not be effective for this architecture.

Tip: For global edge security, always block unwanted traffic using AWS WAF rules at either CloudFront or the ALB, as this prevents threats as early as possible in the request path.

The write-through caching approach guarantees that any modifications in the database are immediately reflected in the cache. As soon as a customer adds or modifies data in the database, the cache is updated accordingly. This ensures strong consistency—what's in the cache always mirrors the underlying database content.

  • Configure a lazy loading cache strategy. - Lazy loading only populates the cache when a read request occurs for missing data; it is possible for the cache to have outdated data if the database is modified outside of the cache's read flow, leading to potential inconsistencies.
  • Introduce a cache with a time-to-live (TTL) policy. - A TTL setting causes items to expire after a set duration, but does not guarantee that the cache will always be in sync with the database—there can still be a window in which the data is stale.
  • Use the AWS AppConfig caching method. - AWS AppConfig is a service for deploying application configuration, not for application data caching; it is irrelevant to the use case described.

Tip: For strict consistency between cache and database, write-through (or write-around) caching is a best practice as it tightly couples cache updates to database changes.

To address the need for automatic 30-day retention and subsequent deletion of S3 backup objects, the best approach is a combination of the following:

  • Enable Object Locking on the S3 bucket. This allows you to enforce retention periods and prevent objects from being deleted or modified within the stipulated time, providing immutability for 30 days.
  • Set a default object retention period of 30 days. With Object Lock enabled, you can specify a default retention period for new objects, ensuring all backups are kept for exactly 30 days.
  • Create an S3 Lifecycle rule to delete objects after 30 days. This automates the removal of objects once the 30-day retention period ends, fulfilling the requirement for automatic deletion.

Why not the other choices?

  • Activate object versioning for the S3 bucket. While versioning helps track object changes and deletions, it does not enforce object retention or automate deletions, and alone does not provide immutability or timed deletion.
  • Set an S3 Lifecycle policy to retain backups for 30 days. Although lifecycle policies can delete objects, they do not prevent deletions before 30 days unless combined with Object Lock; retention enforcement is the critical missing component here.
  • Configure the backup product to add a 30-day retention tag to objects. Adding tags represents metadata only; it does not enforce retention or automate deletion. AWS S3 does not automatically act on these tags without a corresponding lifecycle rule, and it does not ensure the objects are protected.

Tip: When your retention policies require regulatory protection (WORM), always use S3 Object Lock, and combine it with lifecycle policies for automatic expiration. Versioning is important for preservation of old versions but is not a substitute for retention enforcement.

The most effective and cost-efficient approach for improving the performance and availability of a monolithic application running on a single EC2 instance is to first generate an Amazon Machine Image (AMI) of the server and use this in a new launch template. This provides a reusable template to relaunch your application in case of failure or to enable future scaling.

Secondly, you should leverage AWS Compute Optimizer to receive recommendations on better EC2 instance types for vertical scaling. Since the application is monolithic and experiencing high CPU usage, resizing (upgrading) to a larger instance is a practical initial step. Compute Optimizer evaluates your actual workload and suggests the most cost-effective instance size to alleviate bottlenecks.

Why not the other options?
  – Configure an Auto Scaling group and an Application Load Balancer to enable automatic horizontal scaling: Horizontal scaling (adding more instances) is more complex for monolithic applications, as the app may not be designed for distributed workloads. This is less cost-effective initially.
  – Rely on AWS Compute Optimizer to suggest instance types for scaling out horizontally: Compute Optimizer can optimize vertically (bigger/smaller instance), but it does not suggest how to design for horizontal scaling.
  – Establish an Auto Scaling group and an Application Load Balancer, but only to scale the instance vertically: Auto Scaling groups and load balancers are primarily used for horizontal scaling (adding or removing instances), not for vertical scaling. They do not allow you to simply 'scale up' a single instance.

Tips & Tricks:
Vertical scaling is most straightforward for monoliths experiencing high CPU utilization. Create an AMI for rapid redeployment, and use AWS Compute Optimizer for instance sizing. Consider refactoring to microservices for true horizontal scaling in the future.

- Leverage Amazon RDS for MySQL to store critical data, and secure it using AWS KMS client-side encryption. AWS KMS does not natively provide client-side encryption features for RDS, and relying solely on server-side encryption does not guarantee protection from database administrators, who may still query and access contents.

While this offers basic file-level security, it lacks the advanced encryption, access control, and audit features S3 with KMS and bucket policies provide. Windows file permissions may still be circumvented by administrators.

Tip: When securing regulated or highly sensitive data, always use envelope encryption with AWS KMS and manage access using detailed resource policies. Consider using S3 Object Lock or KMS key policies to further prevent unauthorized access, even by high-privilege AWS users.

The correct answer is to Set up an internet-facing Application Load Balancer (ALB) in a public subnet and register the EC2 instance with the ALB’s target group. Make sure the website’s DNS record points to the ALB.

Here's why: Instances launched in private subnets do not have public IP addresses, so they can't accept requests directly from the internet. The standard AWS architecture for exposing resources in a private subnet to the internet is to use an internet-facing ALB (which exists in a public subnet). The ALB can receive internet traffic on behalf of the web server, then forward traffic to EC2 instances running in private subnets.

  • Deploy a NAT gateway in a private subnet, update the private subnet’s route table to point to this gateway, and associate a public Elastic IP address with the NAT gateway. — This is incorrect because a NAT gateway enables outbound internet access for private instances, but it cannot be used to receive inbound traffic from the internet. NAT gateways are not designed to handle or forward unsolicited inbound connections.
  • Adjust the security group of the EC2 instance to allow inbound HTTP (port 80) and HTTPS (port 443) access, and direct the website's DNS record to the instance’s public IP address. — This doesn't work because an instance in a private subnet does not have a public IP. Even with the correct security group rules, internet clients cannot reach it directly.
  • Place the EC2 instance inside an Auto Scaling group in a private subnet, and modify the DNS name for the website to direct traffic to the Auto Scaling group’s identifier. — DNS records cannot resolve to an Auto Scaling group itself, and Auto Scaling groups do not provide an external endpoint. This solution does not make the web servers accessible from the internet.

Tip: In scenarios where private subnets must be maintained for security, pairing them with an ALB is a best practice for exposing internal services securely. Always remember: inbound internet access via NAT Gateway is not possible.

Tips: For scalable and highly available session storage, choose a distributed, in-memory solution with high-availability options and backup capabilities—ElastiCache Redis is purpose-built for this use case.

Implement provisioned concurrency for Lambda guarantees that a chosen number of Lambda instances are always initialized, removing cold starts entirely. However, this approach adds constant additional cost even during periods of low activity and is less cost-effective if strict latency is not mandatory.

Lengthen the Lambda function execution timeout does not affect initialization latency or cold start behavior; it only allows functions to run longer. This setting does not address the latency or scaling concerns in this scenario.

Tip: For Java Lambda functions where you want to reduce cold starts and outlier latencies without high ongoing cost, SnapStart is the optimal choice. Reserve provisioned concurrency for workloads where ultra-low latency is required at all times.

The cluster deployment also offers a dedicated reader endpoint that efficiently load-balances read queries across read-only instances, so you can offload read workloads from the primary DB instance and help reduce costs since you avoid provisioning extra replicas unnecessarily.

  • "Set up an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB instance and direct your read operations to the standby instance within the Multi-AZ configuration." — In Multi-AZ instance deployments, the standby instance is only for failover and does not serve read traffic; it cannot be used to offload reads.
  • "Configure an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB instance deployment, add a read replica, and send your read queries to this replica." — While read replicas can be used for read scaling, this solution uses an RDS instance deployment, not a DB cluster. The failover time is usually longer, and it does not address clustering or cost effectiveness as fully as the DB cluster model does.
  • "Set up an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ DB cluster with two dedicated read replicas and direct read requests to those replicas." — While possible, creating additional dedicated read replicas increases complexity and costs unnecessarily, since the cluster's built-in reader endpoint can distribute reads among already-provisioned reader nodes efficiently.

Tip: For RDS for PostgreSQL workloads that require high availability, low failover downtime, and easy read scaling, Multi-AZ DB clusters with reader endpoints are ideal. Multi-AZ instances serve only as failover targets and do not help scale read workloads.

This prevents anyone, even root, from making unauthorized changes to CloudTrail, thus enforcing the company's required security posture.

The other options are less effective or technically invalid:

  • Define a service-linked role for CloudTrail with a policy permitting alterations only from a specific ARN belonging to the management account. — Service-linked roles can't be used to restrict root access to CloudTrail configuration, nor do ARN conditions prevent root from making changes.
  • Generate a policy in IAM that denies changes to CloudTrail and apply it directly to the root user. — IAM policies cannot be directly attached to the AWS root user. Only SCPs can restrict root's actions at the account level within an organization.
  • Within each developer's account, establish a new CloudTrail trail using the organizational trails feature. — While this helps with centralized logging, it does not prevent trail modifications by account administrators or root users unless further controls like SCPs are in place.

Tip: Use SCPs for security requirements that must override root and administrator permissions in AWS Organizations. Remember that SCPs set the maximum permissions available in an account—they do not grant permissions but rather restrict them.

The optimal solution is to choose Set up provisioned concurrency for the Lambda functions and increase the memory size as recommended by AWS Compute Optimizer. This ensures that Lambda functions start quickly during periods of high traffic (as provisioned concurrency keeps a set number of instances ready to handle requests), preventing cold starts. Increasing the memory allocated—especially as guided by AWS Compute Optimizer—will also proportionally increase the CPU share, thereby speeding up the execution of CPU-intensive code. Faster execution leads to lower compute costs and helps to maintain low latency for end users.

Why are the other choices less effective?

  • Apply reserved concurrency to the Lambda functions while reducing their allocated memory: Lowering memory assignment reduces the CPU, which slows down CPU-intensive tasks. Reserved concurrency only limits executions and does not address cold starts or latency.
  • Implement reserved concurrency for the Lambda functions and raise the memory allocation in line with AWS Compute Optimizer guidance: Increasing memory will help performance, but reserved concurrency does not keep warm instances running, so it does not address the startup latency issue during sudden spikes.
  • Use provisioned concurrency for the Lambda functions, but decrease the memory assigned to them: Provisioned concurrency ensures fast launches, but reducing memory lowers CPU allocation, extending execution time and potentially raising total compute cost.

Tip: For high-concurrency, performance-critical Lambda workloads, always evaluate both concurrency type and memory allocation. Right-sizing memory can actually lower costs by decreasing execution time, especially for CPU-intensive processes!
